bio.en: Christian Idiodi is a partner at Silicon Valley Product Group alongside Marty Cagan, known as “the most interesting man in the world,” helping companies implement and improve the discipline of product management.
bio.zh: Christian Idiodi 是硅谷产品集团（Silicon Valley Product Group）的合伙人，与 Marty Cagan 共事，被称为“世界上最有趣的人”，帮助各公司落地并改进产品管理的纪律。

summary.en: Christian reframes the essence of product management as waking up on behalf of someone else to solve a problem well enough that they give something back, and tackles why the field is so often disliked. He spends significant time on coaching—how to coach your reports and get better coaching from your manager—plus tactics for building trust with leaders. The conversation also shares his single favorite discovery method for figuring out what to build.
summary.zh: Christian 把产品管理的本质重新定义为“替别人醒来、把问题解决好到对方愿意回馈”，并探讨了该领域为何常被人嫌弃。他花大量时间讲教练——如何辅导下属、以及如何从经理那里得到更好的辅导——以及赢得领导者信任的战术。对话还分享了他最偏爱、用来判断“该造什么”的发现方法。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: I try to explain to people that the real essence of this job is that you wake up on behalf of someone else to solve a problem for them, and you have to do it well enough that they give you something back in return. That's kind of the real essence of it, and that's, I always call it a certificate of appreciation. And it could be in the form of revenue, engagement, loyalty, reference, all of those things. And that's the real essence of this job. If it's not fun, you're probably not doing it right. If it's not had, you're probably also not doing it right.
turns.zh: 我试图向人们解释，这份工作的真正本质是，你代表别人醒来，为他们解决问题，而且你必须做得足够好，他们才会给你一些回报。这就是它的真正本质，我总是称其为感谢状。它可以是收入、参与度、忠诚度、推荐度等所有形式。这就是这项工作的真正本质。如果它不有趣，那么你可能没有做对。如果没有，您可能也没有做得正确。

turns.zh: 你们彼此都非常友善。我想从我在产品管理中注意到的这一趋势以及对产品管理的看法开始。感觉就像，我不知道这是新的还是一直存在，但感觉人们有一种不喜欢产品经理的趋势。有一种趋势是，创始人觉得他们应该等待很长时间才能聘请第一位产品经理。有很多团队希望他们的团队中没有产品经理。我们没有这个人告诉我们该做什么。我很好奇你为什么认为人们常常不喜欢产品经理。然后，对于 PM 们的聆听，您对如何不成为人们不喜欢且不希望加入团队的产品经理有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: I think most people don't like product managers often because they haven't experienced good product managers. The core of product management is competency-based, meaning there is someone in an organization that represents the customer the best, that has a deep knowledge of the customers and your users, that has a deep knowledge of your data, your industry, your business and the product itself. And because of this competence, you kind of trust them to make decisions because if you have a problem that says, say we want more customers, it makes a lot of sense to go to the person that is an expert in customers to say, "Help me solve this problem." What you see happening in many organizations is that there is kind of this misperception displaced influence and mistrust because of the poor competency, meaning I feel I know more about the business or I know more about the customer or the data. And so why should I not tell you what to do? (00:06:03): And I think people fail to understand that this role is, it's a team spot. They are part of a team of people working together to discover a solution we're building and in a way that works for our company. And so I think when I think through the companies I've worked with, where I see this discipline really eroded is where there is just not a competent level of product management. The way I describe it to a CEO, I'll ask him, "Tell me who you trust in your company to make a decision on what markets we go to, what things we do." And they always have some senior leader, some VP, some person. And I say, "Why? Oh, Bob has been here a long time. He knows everybody. Everybody loves him and trusts him. He understands our business." And I often say to him, I say, "Well, Bob said put up manager." And it's often interesting to executives when I try to explain that way. I say that's the competent level that we're talking about here. (00:07:01): Imagine if you had Bob's on every team. Imagine how much you can accomplish. So one, I don't really think it's... I often say it's not the hate for product management, it's a hate for the understanding of what they have experienced in product management, which are people that are not able to deliver results that help them meet the outcomes they want. (00:07:23): So if I were advising product managers, I often say, look, when we see sales or executive driven product management where we see these alternatives to product management, it's not a cultural knock or a leadership knock, it's really on the individual and the discipline has to elevate itself to a place that it earns the right to make a decision on what we do.
turns.zh: 我想大多数人不喜欢产品经理往往是因为没有经历过好的产品经理。产品管理的核心是基于能力的，这意味着组织中有人最能代表客户，对客户和用户有深入的了解，对你的数据、你的行业、你的业务和产品本身有深入的了解。由于这种能力，你有点相信他们会做出决定，因为如果你遇到一个问题，比如说我们想要更多的客户，那么去找客户专家说“帮我解决这个问题”是很有意义的。您在许多组织中看到的情况是，由于能力差，这种误解取代了影响和不信任，这意味着我觉得我对业务了解更多，或者我对客户或数据了解更多。那么我为什么不告诉你该怎么做呢？ (00:06:03)：我认为人们无法理解这个角色，它是一个团队位置。他们是团队的一员，他们共同努力发现我们正在构建的解决方案，并以适合我们公司的方式。因此，我认为，当我仔细思考与我合作过的公司时，我发现这一纪律真正受到侵蚀的地方是产品管理水平不高。我向首席执行官描述这一点时，我会问他：“告诉我，你信任公司中的谁来决定我们进入哪些市场，我们做什么。”他们总是有一些高级领导、一些副总裁、一些人。我说：“为什么？哦，鲍勃在这里已经很长时间了。他认识每个人。每个人都爱他并信任他。他了解我们的业务。”我经常对他说，“好吧，鲍勃说的是经理。”当我尝试以这种方式解释时，高管们通常会很感兴趣。我说这就是我们这里所说的胜任水平。 (00:07:01)：想象一下如果每个团队都有鲍勃。想象一下你能完成多少事情。所以，我真的不认为这是......我经常说这不是对产品管理的仇恨，而是对他们在产品管理中所经历的理解的仇恨，这些人无法交付帮助他们实现他们想要的结果的结果。 (00:07:23)：所以，如果我为产品经理提供建议，我经常说，看，当我们看到销售或执行驱动的产品管理时，我们看到这些产品管理的替代方案，这不是文化冲击或领导力冲击，这实际上是针对个人的，并且纪律必须将自己提升到一个位置，使其有权对我们的工作做出决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have exactly the same perspective. When people say they don't like product managers, exactly what I tell them is, you just haven't worked with a great product manager. A great PM makes everything easier for you. If you want to be a PM, people would hate to lose on their team. I would never want to lose Christian on my team as a PM. Is there something they could do maybe or change to become that person?
turns.zh: 我也有完全相同的观点。当人们说他们不喜欢产品经理时，我告诉他们的是，你只是没有和一位优秀的产品经理一起工作。优秀的产品经理会让您的一切变得更加轻松。如果你想成为一名产品经理，人们会不愿意在团队中失败。我永远不想在我的团队中失去克里斯蒂安作为总理。他们可以做些什么或改变来成为那个人吗？

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: Well, I was just joking with someone earlier. I said, "I've only seen great product managers come out of two places. One, either a series of massive failure in their career or experiences that have been bad or from learning from great product leaders." The reality of this kind of role, it's kind of like if you have all kinds of... maybe you're like on a sport, like a quarterback on a team, you need to practice product management to be good at product management. You're not going to get mastery by avoiding some of these elements. (00:08:39): And we've kind of clearly defined what you need to represent to a company for them to trust you. So there is this period of humility that I challenge all product managers to have, this period of learning, recognizing what you do not know. And what you do not have is the trust of an organization or even in yourself that you know the customer, the business or the data better than anybody else. What you need to do is quickly try to accelerate that. You're going to find the loudest, most influential person in your organization, the person that everybody knows, knows everything, is in every meeting and stuff, and you're going to ask them to teach you. You're going to challenge them. And if they don't have the time to teach you, you're going to volunteer to help them. I'm going to intern for you. You're going to get permission from your manager and say, "Look, I want to spend time with Lenny. He's the head of sales, he's the head of operations and stuff. I just want to learn from him." (00:09:35): Now, what you're doing is you're extending that person's trust to yourself. You're also building a relationship with that person. But more importantly, you're learning what is driving that person's influence, which is their competence in the business or the customer. (00:09:51): After you've done that, you have to keep doing discovery because what's going to be different now is that person knows they've taught you everything that they know, but everybody now sees you learning every single day. So at some point, people will recognize that you might have more insights and more data than anybody else, and they will only know this because they've seen you learn from the best and they've seen you continuing to learn. So I always practically advise product managers in this kind of scenario, build relationships with people. You earn their trust by asking them to do two things. One, you're either going to teach me or I'm going to help you. And you're going to build relationships there, gain experience with them. You've got to immerse yourself in the deeper understanding of the business and the data.
turns.zh: 好吧，我之前只是和某人开玩笑。我说：“我只见过两个地方出现了优秀的产品经理。一个是职业生涯中一系列巨大的失败，或者是糟糕的经历，或者是向优秀的产品领导者学习。”这种角色的现实情况，有点像如果你有各种各样的……也许你就像一项运动，就像一支球队的四分卫，你需要练习产品管理才能擅长产品管理。通过避免其中一些元素，您不会获得精通。 (00:08:39)：我们已经明确定义了您需要向公司展示什么，才能让他们信任您。因此，我向所有产品经理提出了这一阶段的谦逊要求，即学习的阶段，认识到自己不知道的东西。而你所缺乏的是组织的信任，甚至是你自己的信任，即你比其他任何人都更了解客户、业务或数据。你需要做的就是快速尝试加速这一过程。你会发现你的组织中声音最大、最有影响力的人，每个人都认识的人，知道一切，参加每次会议和其他事情，你会请他们来教你。你要挑战他们。如果他们没有时间教你，你就会自愿帮助他们。我去给你实习。你需要得到经理的许可，然后说：“听着，我想和莱尼共度时光。他是销售主管，他是运营主管等等。我只是想向他学习。” (00:09:35)：现在，您正在做的就是将他人的信任延伸到您自己。您也在与那个人建立关系。但更重要的是，您正在了解是什么推动了该人的影响力，即他们在业务或客户方面的能力。 (00:09:51)：完成此操作后，您必须继续进行发现，因为现在不同的是，人们知道他们已经教给您他们所知道的一切，但现在每个人都看到您每天都在学习。因此，在某些时候，人们会认识到你可能比其他人拥有更多的见解和更多的数据，他们只会知道这一点，因为他们看到你向最优秀的人学习，并且看到你继续学习。因此，在这种情况下，我总是建议产品经理与人建立关系。你可以通过要求他们做两件事来赢得他们的信任。第一，要么你来教我，要么我来帮助你。你将在那里建立关系，获得与他们的经验。您必须深入了解业务和数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, there's a lot there. Because this is awesome. This is exactly, I think what people want to hear is how do you become better and how do you become more trusted and respected? So things you're recommending to PMs that want to become better, less disliked, more successful. I just took some notes as you were talking. One is there's a sense of becoming more full stack in the company, like understand the business, not just there's your one product and here's your one goal. And then this idea of just be always learning, which is both you are learning things and also people see that you're learning and see that you really care about a lot of the parts of the business that maybe you wouldn't naturally be inclined to understand. And that also helps you build relationships. And also just this really important point of if you know more than anyone else, people will innately trust you and respect you and want you on the team because you happen to have a lot of answers.
turns.zh: 哇，那里有很多。因为这太棒了。这正是，我想人们想听到的是你如何变得更好，你如何变得更值得信任和尊重？所以你向那些想要变得更好、更少不受欢迎、更成功的产品经理推荐的东西。我只是在你说话的时候做了一些笔记。一是公司有一种变得更加全栈的感觉，比如了解业务，而不仅仅是你的一种产品和你的一个目标。然后就是永远学习的想法，即你在学习东西，人们也看到你在学习，看到你真的关心业务的很多部分，而这些部分你可能自然不会倾向于理解。这也可以帮助您建立关系。还有一点非常重要，如果你比其他人知道的更多，人们会天生信任你、尊重你并希望你加入团队，因为你碰巧有很多答案。

And I thought it'd be cool just to spend a little time here. There's these four attributes you guys like to share. Can you just talk about that, as a little foundational?

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: I kind of mentioned before, a product manager is in a team spor., so they work as part of a team to uncover a solution, what to build. And every time you solve a problem, there's inherent risk involved. There's the risk of will people buy this or will they choose it or will they choose to use it, which is all a value type of risk. There's the risk of can they use it, which is a usability type of risk. The risk that we can build it to have the skills to build it or the time to build this, that's a feasibility risk. (00:12:14): And the risk of it working for our business, which is a viability risk. I cannot call out the product manager's competency. It's really to try to drive the first and the last one, which is value and viability. A solution worth building, something people will buy, choose or use, and one that works for our business, which is at the core of what product teams do, solve a problem in a way customers will love and a way that works for our business. It's why the product manager gets all the rap of, if everything goes great, a great team effort, if everything goes wrong, they blame the product manager. (00:12:49): It's because people hold them accountable to results. Nobody wants to work on something nobody wanted in the first place and your job is to ensure that we are working on something people want in the first place. And it is such an amazing role. I try to explain to people that the real essence of this job is that you wake up on behalf of someone else to solve a problem for them. And what an amazing job. There's just no greater... I cannot think of a better discipline with such inherent permission to solve problems on behalf of someone. And you have to do it well enough that they give you something back in return. That's the real essence of it, and that's the, I always call it a certificate of appreciation. And it could be in the form of revenue, engagement, loyalty, reference, all of those things. And that's the real essence of this job. If it's not fun, you're probably not doing it right. If it's not hard, you're probably also not doing it right.
turns.zh: 我之前提到过，产品经理属于团队运动，因此他们作为团队的一部分工作，以发现解决方案，构建什么。每次解决问题时，都会涉及固有的风险。存在人们会购买它、选择它还是选择使用它的风险，这些都是价值类型的风险。存在他们能否使用它的风险，这是一种可用性类型的风险。我们可以构建它以拥有构建它的技能或构建它的时间的风险，这就是可行性风险。 (00:12:14)：以及它对我们的业务起作用的风险，即生存风险。我无法说出产品经理的能力。真正是要努力推动第一个和最后一个，也就是价值和生存能力。一个值得构建的解决方案，人们会购买、选择或使用的解决方案，并且适合我们的业务，这是产品团队工作的核心，以客户喜欢的方式解决问题，并且适合我们的业务。这就是为什么产品经理会得到大家的赞誉，如果一切顺利，那就是团队的努力，如果一切出了问题，他们就会责怪产品经理。 (00:12:49)：这是因为人们要求他们对结果负责。没有人愿意做一些本来就没有人想要的事情，而你的工作就是确保我们首先做的是人们想要的事情。这是一个非常了不起的角色。我试图向人们解释，这份工作的真正本质是你代表别人醒来，为他们解决问题。这是多么了不起的工作啊。没有比这更伟大的了……我想不出还有比这更好的学科了，它具有如此内在的权限来代表某人解决问题。你必须做得足够好，他们才会给你一些回报。这就是它的真正本质，这就是，我总是称其为感谢状。它可以是收入、参与度、忠诚度、推荐度等所有形式。这就是这项工作的真正本质。如果它不有趣，那么你可能没有做对。如果这并不难，那么你可能也没有做对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I love that frame of reference of you're giving something to customers and your success is measured by do they give something back in return, which is basically do they pay for your product? Such a beautiful way to think about that. Oh, man. (00:14:05): Okay. So just to summarize these four elements, there's value, usability, viability, feasibility to understand if the product they're building hits all these attributes.
turns.zh: 哇，我喜欢你为客户提供一些东西的参考框架，而你的成功是通过他们是否给予回报来衡量的，这基本上就是他们为你的产品付费吗？这是一个多么美妙的思考方式。哦，伙计。 (00:14:05)：好的。因此，总结一下这四个要素，即价值、可用性、生存能力、可行性，以了解他们正在构建的产品是否满足所有这些属性。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: That's right. You're trying to uncover a solution and you know you've solved the problem when you get those two things, something customers love, they give you something back, and our business can support it in some ways. And I'm calling out, these are the different risks in our kind of taxonomy, how we call the things you have to tackle. And it's a team sport, and so there are these four risks of should we build it, will people use it, will people buy it, will our customers support it or our business support it? And you're trying to answer those questions with a designer and a product engineer.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。你试图找到一个解决方案，当你得到这两件事时，你知道你已经解决了问题，客户喜欢的东西，他们给你一些回报，我们的业务可以以某种方式支持它。我要指出的是，这些是我们分类法中的不同风险，我们如何称呼你必须解决的事情。这是一项团队运动，因此存在四个风险：我们是否应该构建它、人们会使用它、人们会购买它、我们的客户会支持它还是我们的业务会支持它？您正在尝试与设计师和产品工程师一起回答这些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of these four, so value, usability, viability, feasibility, where do you think most new PMs fail most or should spend more time?
turns.zh: 在这四个方面，即价值、可用性、生存能力、可行性，您认为大多数新产品经理在哪些方面最失败或者应该花更多时间？

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: Oh my goodness, value. Value is probably, it is the most important and the most overlooked. And the big driver for that is often because of the operating model of teams. Teams are often given roadmaps of projects and features to go build and deliver. If that's the case, you actually really don't need a product manager because they're going to assume value. If the boss told me to build this, I cannot say, "Should we build this? Is this the right thing to build? Is there a better option? Is this what people will buy?" You just assume it's valuable. (00:15:38): And so often, when people ask me why does the product manager seem to play like a core leadership role on a team, almost like the quarterback. And it's not that they're more special in solving the problem that the designer or the engineer, but they're answering a question that determines if we should be working on this in the first place. (00:15:57): So value is often the hardest thing to solve and must be overlooked. We often see bad patterns where companies will say, "Yes, we ran a test, with 300 users and they all scored it 84% or 90%. They love it." In that way. I said, "Well, just because somebody can use your product doesn't mean that they will buy it. Just because they can use it doesn't mean they will choose it. Just because they can use it doesn't mean that they will actually use it." And what people say is often different from what they do. And our job is to actually solve the problem, which is what core value is, in a meaningful way. And often overlooked because we check the box on our own item. So the most important, because that's to the point of the certificate of appreciation, what you get in return, that's the ultimate outcome. Really, value.
turns.zh: 天哪，值。价值可能是最重要的，也是最容易被忽视的。其主要驱动因素通常是团队的运营模式。团队通常会获得要构建和交付的项目和功能的路线图。如果是这样的话，你实际上真的不需要产品经理，因为他们会承担价值。如果老板让我建造这个，我不能说：“我们应该建造这个吗？建造这个东西正确吗？有更好的选择吗？人们会买这个吗？”你只是假设它有价值。 (00:15:38)：很多时候，当人们问我为什么产品经理似乎在团队中扮演着核心领导角色，几乎就像四分卫一样。并不是说他们在解决问题方面比设计师或工程师更特别，而是他们正在回答一个决定我们是否应该首先解决这个问题的问题。 (00:15:57)：所以价值往往是最难解决的问题，必须被忽视。我们经常看到一些不好的模式，公司会说：“是的，我们对 300 名用户进行了测试，他们的得分都是 84% 或 90%。他们喜欢这样。”就这样。我说，“嗯，仅仅因为有人可以使用你的产品并不意味着他们会购买它。仅仅因为他们可以使用它并不意味着他们会选择它。仅仅因为他们可以使用它并不意味着他们会真正使用它。”人们所说的往往与他们所做的不同。我们的工作是以有意义的方式实际解决问题，这就是核心价值。而且经常被忽视，因为我们在自己的项目上勾选了复选框。所以最重要的是，因为这关系到感谢状，你得到的回报，这就是最终的结果。真的，值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You once gave a talk along these lines around discovery, and it was this talk of here's all of the things you can do to help understand what to build to make something valuable. There's a billion frameworks for every step of the discovery process, press releases, story mapping, opportunity solution, trees, fake door tests, all these things. And you're like, if we had to pick one thing, if there's one process or approach that you recommend most, your answer was essentially finding some number of reference customers to work with and helping them and working with them to design the product. Do you still see that as the one, if you had to pick one approach to figure out what to build? And if so, you just talk about how you recommend going about that.
turns.zh: 您曾经就发现问题做过一次演讲，这次演讲讨论了您可以做的所有事情，以帮助理解构建什么来使某些东西变得有价值。发现过程的每一步、新闻稿、故事映射、机会解决方案、树、假门测试，所有这些都有十亿个框架。你会想，如果我们必须选择一件事，如果有一种你最推荐的流程或方法，那么你的答案本质上就是找到一些可以合作的参考客户，帮助他们并与他们一起设计产品。如果您必须选择一种方法来弄清楚要构建什么，您仍然认为这是一种方法吗？如果是这样，你只需谈谈你建议如何去做。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: The holy grail of product walk is really a reference customer. This is somebody that has used your solution or your product, loves it enough to tell people about it. I kind of described the work of the product team is to solve problems in a way that customers love and a way that works for our business. The ultimate definition for me today of the love that somebody has for our product is they're willing to put their reputation on the line by telling people about it. And for me, if we think about you do a lot of interviews with founders and entrepreneurs and you're going to have people that they find a market with an idea and they jump in. But if you think at the core of some of these founder-inspired businesses where the founder will say, "Well, I had a problem and it was their problem and they focused on solving the problem and then they got their friends on it." (00:18:39): And so it's almost like this idea that if they were their own first reference customer. They were so close to the problem, immersed in the environment of the problem, solved it in a compelling way enough where it was like, there are more people like me. And it is like if I said to you, "Lenny, let's go to a steakhouse. Find me a new steakhouse around you." You might go online and Google and you see a steakhouse with one review. How do you feel about that? I don't know. Maybe other people don't want to try this. You see two reviews, you're like, maybe it's the chef and their spouse or something. The question is how many positive reviews would you have to see to jump and say, "Let's go try this one." There are some things inherent in, if you look at Geoffrey Moore's adoption curve and those kinds of models in here, most people don't want to be the first to try things. But you are likely to try things if other people that look like you have accepted it or defined it as good. (00:19:39): And so the whole essence for me of this technique is to create those first people, those reference customers. If you think about how companies make the shift to becoming sales-led or operations-led, almost all companies start product-led. The product is first. You kind of build something and it's like, yeah, it's going, let's hire salespeople and marketing people and operational people to do it. What's really happening is that the product team created the first customers. And now a group of people have to capture the value that was created. So what's happening here is that it is constantly the job of product teams. The reason they lose influence is because salespeople are having to sell a product. You see? So they're like forcing back, "I need this and I need this." But if you came to me and said, "I want to buy steak," and I say, "Let me show you 20 people that look like you that recommend this steakhouse," my job as a salesperson is very easy. I'm just like, "Hey, you should eat here. Everybody that loves steak, they all eat here." (00:20:44): So product teams feel, at this contract to an organization when they don't create powerful reference customers. So it's by far my favorite technique. And the way this technique works is you want to discover and deliver and develop who has the problem, the customer. I want to discover who has the problem. At the same time, discover and deliver a solution to this problem. The idea here is that if you really want to solve a problem, you need to get out of your building. Go spend time with someone that has the problem and don't leave until you solve the problem. People talk about why we had such a record time to the Covid vaccine. Sure, technology has improved, our research has improved. But if you think about it, we had the highest number of volunteers for vaccination in the history of any vaccine in the history of time. (00:21:36): Why? Did we have to look for someone with Covid? No, they were literally all around us. The research was immersed in the environment of the problem. They could study... and so this is often what I call, it's almost like a pressure-cooked discovery in some ways. If you truly, truly want to solve a problem, get out of your building, get out of the assumptions, get out of your opinions. Immerse yourself, find someone who has the problem, stick with them until you discover a solution for this problem. And you're going to do that. The part of why I love this technique, the two biggest reasons I think, the first is if I cannot find a certain number of people that have this problem, my goodness, it might not be a problem, but solve it. I have never had a product failure using this technique. If I were to credit... goodness, I think last count, I'm up to like 205 products I have worked on or participated in creating in my career. And I tried to build a new product every year from scratch. It's kind of a crazy thing about me. My friends know what I want for my bad day is a problem worth solving. And I like to go from idea to revenue, and the setup, and I test all of these techniques in this way. And everybody knows my favorite technique is if we find a problem worth solving, we need to uncover a solution for B2B, I want six to eight references, for B2C, I want maybe 15 to 25 references as an indication that we've achieved product market fit.
turns.zh: 产品行走的圣杯确实是参考客户。这是使用过您的解决方案或产品的人，非常喜欢它并愿意向人们介绍它。我描述了产品团队的工作就是以客户喜欢的、适合我们业务的方式解决问题。今天，对我来说，人们对我们产品的热爱的最终定义是，他们愿意冒着声誉风险，向人们介绍我们的产品。对我来说，如果我们对创始人和企业家进行大量采访，你就会发现人们找到了一个有想法的市场，然后他们就加入了。但如果你想想这些受创始人启发的企业的核心，创始人会说，“嗯，我遇到了一个问题，这是他们的问题，他们专注于解决问题，然后他们让他们的朋友解决这个问题。” (00:18:39)：如果他们是自己的第一个参考客户，这几乎就像这个想法。他们如此接近问题，沉浸在问题的环境中，以足够引人注目的方式解决它，就像，有更多像我这样的人。就好像我对你说：“莱尼，我们去一家牛排馆吧。给我在你周围找一家新的牛排馆。”你可能会上网和谷歌，然后你会看到一家牛排馆有一条评论。你对此有何感想？我不知道。也许其他人不想尝试这个。你看到两条评论，你会想，也许是厨师和他们的配偶之类的。问题是你必须看到多少正面评论才能跳起来说：“我们去试试这个吧。”如果你看看杰弗里摩尔的采用曲线和这里的那些模型，有一些固有的东西，大多数人不想成为第一个尝试的人。但如果其他看起来像你的人已经接受了某件事或将其定义为好的事情，你就可能会尝试。 (00:19:39)：所以对我来说，这项技术的全部本质就是创造第一批人，那些参考客户。如果您考虑公司如何转变为销售主导或运营主导，那么几乎所有公司都是从产品主导开始的。产品是第一位的。你建造了一些东西，然后就好像，是的，它正在进行，让我们雇佣销售人员、营销人员和运营人员来做这件事。真正发生的事情是产品团队创建了第一批客户。现在，一群人必须捕捉所创造的价值。因此，这里发生的事情始终是产品团队的工作。他们失去影响力的原因是销售人员必须销售产品。你看？所以他们就像强行反击，“我需要这个，我需要这个。”但如果你来找我说，“我想买牛排”，我说，“让我向你展示 20 个看起来像你的人推荐这家牛排馆”，我作为销售人员的工作就非常简单了。我只是想，“嘿，你应该在这里吃饭。每个喜欢牛排的人，他们都在这里吃。” (00:20:44)：因此，当产品团队没有创建强大的参考客户时，他们就会觉得与组织签订了这份合同。所以这是迄今为止我最喜欢的技术。这种技术的工作方式是你想要发现、交付和开发有问题的人，即客户。我想找出谁有问题。同时，发现并提供解决该问题的方案。这里的想法是，如果你真的想解决问题，你需要离开你的大楼。花时间与有问题的人在一起，直到解决问题为止。人们谈论为什么我们的新冠疫苗接种时间如此之长。当然，技术进步了，我们的研究也进步了。但如果你想一想，我们的疫苗接种志愿者数量是有史以来疫苗接种史上最多的。 (00:21:36)：为什么？我们必须寻找感染新冠病毒的人吗？不，他们确实就在我们周围。研究沉浸在问题的环境中。他们可以研究……所以这通常是我所说的，在某些方面它几乎就像是一个高压煮的发现。如果你真的真的想解决问题，就走出你的大楼，摆脱假设，摆脱你的观点。让自己沉浸其中，找到有问题的人，坚持下去，直到找到解决该问题的方法。你会这么做的。我喜欢这个技术的部分原因，我认为有两个最大的原因，第一是如果我找不到一定数量的人有这个问题，天哪，这可能不是问题，而是解决它。我使用这种技术从未出现过产品故障。如果我要相信……天哪，我想最后统计一下，在我的职业生涯中，我已经开发或参与创造了大约 205 个产品。我每年都尝试从头开始开发一款新产品。这对我来说有点疯狂。我的朋友们知道我在糟糕的一天想要什么是一个值得解决的问题。我喜欢从想法到收入，再到设置，我以这种方式测试所有这些技术。每个人都知道我最喜欢的技术是，如果我们发现一个值得解决的问题，我们需要找到 B2B 的解决方案，我想要六到八个参考，对于 B2C，我可能想要 15 到 25 个参考，以表明我们已经实现了产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to be clear, you said you still work, you build products yourself and you practice this and you've built... okay, what's like every recent product that you've built? I didn't know this.
turns.zh: 需要澄清的是，您说过您仍在工作，您自己构建产品，您实践了这一点，并且您已经构建了......好吧，您最近构建的每个产品是什么样的？我不知道这个。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: So I do a lot of work in Africa now. WorkNigeria is like a job board that helps people. We do kind of a job board HR replacement and advisory too as well. I'm actually working on another app around the NDA and protecting high-asset individuals in some ways. So kind of every year, I find a problem like that worth solving and I practice doing the work of discovery with a team of people.
turns.zh: 所以我现在在非洲做了很多工作。 WorkNigeria 就像一个帮助人们的工作委员会。我们也提供招聘委员会人力资源更换和咨询服务。实际上，我正在围绕 NDA 开发另一个应用程序，并以某种方式保护高资产个人。每年，我都会发现一个值得解决的问题，并且我会与一群人一起练习发现工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. I see this unraveling of the most interesting man in the world is happening a little, bit by bit. We learn more and more about you. Okay, amazing. So just to kind of summarize some of these-
turns.zh: 太棒了。我看到这个世界上最有趣的人的真相正在一点一点地发生。我们越来越了解您。好吧，太棒了。所以只是总结一下其中的一些 -

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, amazing. So just to summarize some of these points, which are really great and I've never heard it described this way before. So basically, a really effective way to understand how to build something people actually want and solve real problems is this idea of pick reference customers. And I really like this word reference, which is not just they're going to help you build a thing, but they're also become a reference to future customers because they end up loving it because you built it for them and they love it. (00:24:27): Your advice is find six to eight in B2B space, 15 to 25 in B2C. And the reason there's a number here is if you find just one or two, you never know, they might be just the one or two that have this really weird problem that no one else has. And I think that's usually the flaw in this approach is you end up building it for a small number of people and nobody else really wants it. And it sounds like in your experience, this is a good kind of number where probably a lot of more people will have this problem.
turns.zh: 好吧，太棒了。总结一下其中的一些观点，这些观点真的很棒，我以前从未听过这样的描述。因此，基本上，了解如何构建人们真正想要的东西并解决实际问题的真正有效的方法是选择参考客户的想法。我真的很喜欢这个词参考，这不仅仅是他们会帮助你构建一个东西，而且他们也成为未来客户的参考，因为他们最终会喜欢它，因为你为他们构建了它并且他们喜欢它。 (00:24:27)：您的建议是在 B2B 领域找到 6 到 8 个，在 B2C 领域找到 15 到 25 个。这里有一个数字的原因是，如果你只发现一两个，你永远不知道，他们可能只是一两个遇到其他人没有的非常奇怪的问题。我认为这种方法的缺陷通常是你最终为少数人构建了它，而没有其他人真正想要它。听起来根据您的经验，这是一个很好的数字，可能会有更多的人遇到这个问题。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: Yeah. There've been studies to validate some of these numbers. I think early, IBM, kind of struggled selling those supercomputers. And if you're buying a million dollar computer, someone says, "Hey, do you want to buy?" And you're like, "I don't know. Is there anybody else that has bought it? Shall I be the first?" And there was this common question of what would it take for you to buy it? And someone says, "Hey, if I see five or six people that look like me already have this, then I feel confident making the argument to my company, we should jump on it." And it's like, so how do I create the first five to six? And you can see a lot of the validation on B2C in some of the things you might see in the App Store on Yelp or those places. My idea here is if you found a steakhouse with 25 5-star reviews, you are likely to adopt this. (00:25:41): So in every app I have ever put on the App Store, on the day I launch the app in the app store, they are 25 5-star reviews. I will never launch an app and be like, "Let's hope Lenny loves it. Let's see who the first person." On the very first day of launching the app, there are 25... so I will know I am not ready until I have achieved 25 people that have told me, worked with me and said, "I am now ready to put my reputation the line." Sometimes I might need to work with 30 people or 50 people because the output is 25 reference customers. Because if Lenny is like, "I don't love it enough" or "I don't feel comfortable," I'm not going to customize for Lenny. I'm going to find my single target market, talk to more people. If I get 25, I have achieved product market fit.
turns.zh: 是的。已经有研究验证其中一些数字。我认为早期 IBM 在销售这些超级计算机方面遇到了困难。如果你要买一台价值百万美元的电脑，有人会说：“嘿，你想买吗？”你会说，“我不知道。还有其他人买过吗？我应该是第一个吗？”还有一个常见的问题是您需要什么才能购买它？有人说，“嘿，如果我看到五六个像我一样的人已经有了这个，那么我就有信心向我的公司提出论点，我们应该采取行动。”就像，那么我如何创建前五到六个呢？您可以在 Yelp 或那些地方的 App Store 中看到的一些内容中看到很多 B2C 验证。我的想法是，如果您发现一家有 25 条 5 星级评论的牛排馆，您很可能会采用它。 (00:25:41)：因此，在我放在 App Store 上的每个应用程序中，在我在应用程序商店中启动该应用程序的那天，它们都是 25 条 5 星级评论。我永远不会在启动应用程序时说：“希望莱尼喜欢它。让我们看看谁是第一人。”在推出该应用程序的第一天，就有 25 个人……所以，直到有 25 个人告诉我、与我合作并说“我现在已经准备好以我的声誉为赌注”，我才会知道我还没有准备好。有时我可能需要与 30 人或 50 人一起工作，因为输出是 25 个参考客户。因为如果莱尼说，“我不够喜欢它”或“我感觉不舒服”，我就不会为莱尼定制。我要找到我的单一目标市场，与更多的人交谈。如果我得到 25，我就实现了产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. It basically kicks in this word of mouth flywheel that everyone's always looking for is how do I get people to talk about it. Build it for them, solve their problems, tell them that it exists. You mentioned a bit about how you understand if it's actually, let's call a product market fit, if you have product market fit with these people that you ask them if they're going to leave you a 5-star review for example. I guess what do you consider this is good, I got one more person that's really happy with this? What tells you it's got product market fit with a person?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。它基本上启动了口碑飞轮，每个人一直在寻找的是我如何让人们谈论它。为他们构建它，解决他们的问题，告诉他们它的存在。您提到了一些关于您如何理解的问题，如果实际上，让我们称之为产品市场契合度，如果您的产品市场契合度与这些人相同，那么您会询问他们是否会给您留下 5 星评价。我想你认为这有什么好处，我又多了一个对此感到非常满意的人？什么告诉你它的产品市场适合一个人？

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: If I were thinking about how I will do this, pick a problem to solve, first of all, I have to know who I'm solving the problem for. And in some indication and I want to validate that this is actually a problem you do have. And I'm looking for a certain type of person. These early adopters in our world are broken up to technologists and evangelists. Technologists could be, "I love the new iPhone 16 is coming out and it's going to have five cameras and I write an article in some tech review board. Super fast, super sleek, all good design." You just love new technology. You always jump on new technology. And evangelist could be someone that says, "Oh my, I look great with the iPhone 15, it has three cameras. I will look phenomenal with the iPhone 16, so I'm going to go stand in line at the Apple Store for three hours or overnight because I just can't wait to get my hands on the Apple 16." (00:27:53): They may feel a little irrational, but those are the kind of people you're looking for, people that believe they have a problem. So it's like you will try any steakhouse, in my example. You're just like, "I love steak. I don't care if there are reviews or not. I'll try it." And what I'm trying to do here is I'm saying, okay, Lenny loves steak, he wants to try a steakhouse. And I'm good to say, "Lenny, I'm trying to build the best steakhouse here. If I create a menu that you absolutely love, are you willing to tell people about it?" That could be a video testimonial, write a review, stuff like that. And it's okay Lenny, if you don't love the first iteration of it and stuff like that, I want to hear your feedback. I want you to work with me in ensuring that I build the best steakhouse here. And that's kind of the idea. (00:28:37): So I'm going to work with 25 people that look like you and I'm going to keep tweaking, in this sense iterating on the product and the menu until Lenny's like, "My goodness, this is the best steakhouse in the world." It is like I'm just going to write about it and when I get 25 people that have all, it's not the steakhouse, they love it enough. Because this is where you really get the shift in value. Because if I say, "Lenny, go write me a review, a five-star review." You're like, "I don't know if I feel comfortable about." You say, "Why not?" You see, I'm really going to get deeper feedback because people will say or do anything just to avoid hurting our feelings or for us to get out of their face. So they'll be like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah, I'll give you a five-star review." But when I say do it, you're like, "Well, I have this hesitation." Why? That's really where great discovery comes. But it's hard to in a silo. You have to be immersed with the person that has the problem. So product market fit is when you iterate it in this discovery, you've discovered and delivered something so meaningful that these customers that are your target customers, are willing to put their reputation on the line and be a reference. That's my indication.
turns.zh: 如果我正在考虑如何做到这一点，选择一个要解决的问题，首先，我必须知道我要为谁解决问题。在某些迹象中，我想验证这实际上是您确实遇到的问题。我正在寻找某种类型的人。我们世界上的这些早期采用者分为技术专家和传播者。技术专家可能会说，“我喜欢即将推出的新款 iPhone 16，它将有五个摄像头，我在一些技术评论板上写了一篇文章。超级快，超级时尚，所有设计都很好。”你只是喜欢新技术。你总是会采用新技术。传道者可能会说：“天哪，我用 iPhone 15 看起来很棒，它有三个摄像头。我用 iPhone 16 看起来也很棒，所以我要去 Apple Store 排队三个小时或一整夜，因为我迫不及待地想拿到 Apple 16。” (00:27:53)：他们可能会觉得有点不理性，但这些人就是你要寻找的人，那些相信自己有问题的人。所以在我的例子中，就像你会尝试任何牛排馆一样。你就像，“我喜欢牛排。我不在乎是否有评论。我会尝试一下。”我在这里想做的是，好吧，莱尼喜欢牛排，他想尝试一下牛排馆。我很高兴地说，“莱尼，我正在努力打造这里最好的牛排馆。如果我创建了一份你绝对喜欢的菜单，你愿意告诉人们吗？”这可能是视频推荐、写评论等等。没关系，莱尼，如果你不喜欢它的第一次迭代之类的东西，我想听听你的反馈。我希望你和我一起努力，确保我在这里建造最好的牛排馆。这就是这个想法。 (00:28:37)：所以我将与 25 个看起来像你的人一起工作，我将不断调整，从这个意义上迭代产品和菜单，直到 Lenny 说，“我的天哪，这是世界上最好的牛排馆。”就好像我正要写下它，当我得到 25 个人都拥有的时候，这不是牛排馆，他们足够喜欢它了。因为这是你真正获得价值转变的地方。因为如果我说，“莱尼，去给我写一篇评论，一篇五星级的评论。”你会说，“我不知道我是否感到舒服。”你说：“为什么不呢？”你看，我真的会得到更深入的反馈，因为人们会说或做任何事情只是为了避免伤害我们的感情或让我们从他们面前消失。所以他们会说，“是啊，是啊，是啊，我会给你五星级的评价。”但当我说去做时，你会说，“好吧，我有这个犹豫。”为什么？这确实是伟大发现的来源。但在筒仓里很难做到。你必须沉浸在有问题的人身边。因此，产品市场契合度是指当您在这一发现中重复它时，您发现并交付了一些非常有意义的东西，以至于这些客户（您的目标客户）愿意冒着声誉风险并成为参考。这就是我的指示。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine though, Christian, so charismatic, comes to me and says, "Hey Lenny, would you leave me a five star review for this product. I'm working on this, I'm trying to figure out if people want it." I would be like, "Yeah, of course. I'll leave you a five-star review." What do you do to kind of avoid that, just like I just want to be nice, like I don't care, I'll leave a five-star review.
turns.zh: 但我想，如此有魅力的克里斯蒂安会走过来对我说：“嘿，莱尼，你能给我这个产品五星级的评价吗？我正在研究这个，我正在努力弄清楚人们是否想要它。”我会说，“是的，当然。我会给你五星级的评价。”你会做什么来避免这种情况，就像我只是想表现得友善，就像我不在乎一样，我会留下五星级的评论。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: You. It's part of why I need 25 in B2C. And don't get me wrong, if I can convince 25 people in there, I may have a marketing product and a charismatic marketing products. If that's all I needed to do was a good message and charisma to get people on it. The good benefits of this is that you can tackle risk very early because you can involve many other parts of your organization, marketing, sales, legal, finance. People often ask me how do I come up with the marketing spiel or the description? I'm like, "I don't make that up." If I ask Lenny, "What do you feel about this product?" And he says, "Well, it's cool and it's very sleek and very nice." The marketing department will say, "We don't like those terms. We want to call it comprehensive." And when you go out to sell your product, people are going to be disappointed because the expectations are created by what's on the box. (00:31:04): I only market exactly what customers tell me. I have never been surprised about what customers will say when I release a product because in this technique I already get their feedback. And so I'm going to put exactly what Lenny said on the box. "Hey, this product's cool and sleek and easy to use." I've only launched a product that says super fast but difficult to read because the technology team said there was no way to change the font on something and it was just going to be difficult to read. And you know what everybody did when they got the product? "Oh my goodness, it is super [inaudible 00:31:39]. All right, it is also difficult to read." It matched their expectations in some ways. So what I do here is I learn how to sell the product with this technique, I learn how to market the product because I have real people, that we're not making assumptions. (00:31:54): What's the best way to market this? How much Lenny? How would you find this? Does this language resonate with you? Does this properly describe the menu? See? So that's kind of what you're doing when you use a technique like this. It feels heavy to people, but that's kind of part of the practice of it. If you do this a whole lot, you get really comfortable at involving, you're working with your customers to solve it. But for me, the fact that you will not have a product failure because you have a natural pivot out, meaning if I can't find 25 people that love steak, why in the world am I building a steakhouse? So if you don't find enough people that love this problem and are willing to help you, just be like, this is not a problem worth solving. But more importantly, you really start to get... is the fastest part to product market fit, the clearest definition for me because I know when my product is ready, when I've dotted those I's and crossed those T's, in that way.
turns.zh: 你。这也是我在 B2C 领域需要 25 的部分原因。不要误会我的意思，如果我能说服那里的 25 个人，我可能会拥有一个营销产品和一个有魅力的营销产品。如果这就是我需要做的，那就是一个好的信息和魅力来吸引人们的关注。这样做的好处是，您可以尽早应对风险，因为您可以让组织的许多其他部分参与其中，包括营销、销售、法律、财务。人们经常问我如何提出营销演讲或描述？我想，“这不是我编造的。”如果我问莱尼：“你对这个产品有什么感觉？”他说：“嗯，这很酷，而且非常时尚，非常漂亮。”营销部门会说：“我们不喜欢这些术语。我们想称其为全面的。”当你出去销售你的产品时，人们会感到失望，因为期望是由盒子上的东西创造的。 (00:31:04)：我只营销客户告诉我的内容。当我发布产品时，我从来没有对客户会说什么感到惊讶，因为通过这种技术，我已经得到了他们的反馈。所以我要把莱尼所说的话准确地写在盒子上。 “嘿，这个产品很酷，很时尚，而且很容易使用。”我只推出了一款声称速度超快但难以阅读的产品，因为技术团队表示无法更改某些内容的字体，而且阅读起来会很困难。你知道每个人拿到产品后都做了什么吗？ “天哪，这太棒了 [听不清 00:31:39]。好吧，它也很难读。”它在某些方面符合他们的期望。所以我在这里所做的是学习如何用这种技术销售产品，我学习如何营销产品，因为我有真实的人，我们不会做出假设。 (00:31:54)：营销这个产品的最佳方式是什么？莱尼多少钱？你会如何找到这个？这种语言能引起您的共鸣吗？这是否正确描述了菜单？看？这就是当你使用这样的技术时你正在做的事情。这对人们来说感觉很沉重，但这就是它的实践的一部分。如果你经常这样做，你就会非常轻松地参与其中，并与你的客户一起解决问题。但对我来说，事实上你不会有产品失败，因为你有一个自然的转型，这意味着如果我找不到 25 个喜欢牛排的人，我到底为什么要建造一家牛排馆？因此，如果您没有找到足够多的人喜欢这个问题并愿意帮助您，那就说，这不是一个值得解决的问题。但更重要的是，你真的开始明白……是产品市场契合最快的部分，对我来说是最清晰的定义，因为我知道我的产品何时准备就绪，何时我以这种方式点缀了那些“我”并跨越了那些“T”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think your point there, recruiting is itself a huge signal, is really important. Can you find people that have this problem and care enough about this problem that they're going to talk to you and spend time exploring this thing that doesn't exist yet. I think that's super interesting. And then I think another key part of this is it's one solution that solves many people's problems. And it can't be a bunch of different things for a bunch of different people.
turns.zh: 我认为你的观点是，招聘本身就是一个巨大的信号，非常重要。你能否找到有这个问题并且足够关心这个问题的人，他们会与你交谈并花时间探索这个尚不存在的东西。我认为这非常有趣。我认为另一个关键部分是它是一个解决许多人问题的解决方案。对于一群不同的人来说，它不可能是一堆不同的东西。

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: That's right, that's right. If one person says, "I don't want this," wants this, another person wants this, you don't do it. That's how you know you do the minimum. All 25 have to want the same thing. If one person's out, you just don't do it at all. And the reason that's powerful is because if I come to you and I say, "Hey, it's missing this feature." I say, "Well yeah, 25 people that look like you that are very happy without it." You see? That's how if you think about what you do in a review, you see the five stars and you instantly like, "Oh, that's good enough." But if you have a question, what do you do, you cannot double click on the review to read. And that's how people get convinced. There's this social influence of like, "Well, Lenny's cool, he likes the steakhouse. I should like it. He's fine with this not being there so I should be fine with it." So your references are super powerful in more than any company, in influencing consumers on what they should choose or not choose.
turns.zh: 没错，没错。如果一个人说，“我不想要这个”，想要这个，另一个人想要这个，你就不会这样做。这就是你知道你做了最少的事情的方式。所有 25 个人都想要同样的东西。如果一个人出去了，你就根本不做这件事。它之所以强大，是因为如果我来找你，我说：“嘿，它缺少这个功能。”我说：“嗯，是的，有 25 个人像你一样，没有它也很快乐。”你看？这就是为什么当你思考你在评论中所做的事情时，你会看到五颗星，然后你会立即喜欢，“哦，这已经足够好了。”但如果你有疑问，你该怎么办，你不能双击评论来阅读。这就是人们被说服的方式。有这样的社会影响，“嗯，莱尼很酷，他喜欢牛排馆。我应该喜欢它。他不介意不在那里，所以我应该也同意。”因此，在影响消费者应该选择或不选择什么方面，你的推荐比任何公司都更强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, Strive builds new products exactly this way. They find new customers that have a problem and they work with very small number of customers to build a product for them, and that's how a lot of their new product... I think Rippling works like this too. So I think this is a really good lesson for everyone listening, if they're trying to build something new. Is there an example that comes to mind that would be, I don't know, interesting to talk through, of something you built that you worked through this process?
turns.zh: 基本上，Strive 就是这样构建新产品的。他们找到有问题的新客户，并与极少数客户合作为他们构建产品，这就是他们的很多新产品的方式……我认为 Ripple 也是这样工作的。所以我认为这对于每个听的人来说都是一个非常好的教训，如果他们正在尝试构建新的东西的话。我不知道，是否有一个例子是你在这个过程中构建的、值得讨论的有趣例子？

turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: Oh, boy. I tell the example of solving a problem when I was at a staffing company, a snag job. They do hourly jobs and help people find their best job or an hourly job and I actually get a call here from the head of Global staffing at Starbucks. Now, he called me, you can see the benefit of this technique, because I'm the person he calls when he has problems. I've used this technique with him at a previous company. He didn't even know I was at a new company. And he calls me up and he says, "Christian, I have a problem." I said, "Well, don't we all have problems?" He said, well, "We just bought a bakery in the San Francisco Bay Area. And as we're doing the paperwork to kind of take over this company or this acquisition, we realized that close to 800 of the employees may be undocumented workers." (00:35:22): And I said, "Wow, that does sound like a problem." He's like, "Yeah, imagine if this breaks out in the news and all of that. But more importantly, we still need to get all their paperwork. So all these people are going to quit and we'll have a new bakery without employees." And my first question to him as a product guy is like, "Wow, would you give me a million dollars to solve this problem?" And it's like, "No, seriously?" I was like, "300,000." I'm throwing out numbers. He's like, "Maybe." I said, "Wow, you have my attention." I go to my CEO, I tell him to call. I grab a designer and an engineer. I just say, "Hey look, I would love to work on a little project with you all if you have some time." I kind of debrief them on the call. Now the first thing I have to do is to try to define the problem, identify problems. What really is the problem going on? (00:36:08): Yeah, we're breaking it down, we're talking through this. We say, well, at the end of the day, Starbucks needs to hire like 800 people quickly because we can't fix getting everybody's paperwork. But they're going to lose these people and they need to hire those quickly. And I say, well, who else has this problem? We're trying to throw out guesses. I'm like, "What are we talking about? Let's go out." Everybody jumps in my car and we start driving around and this is where we're doing our product work from. We're talking in the car, just out of the building. We see a new construction site for a new McDonald's coming soon and we're curious. We're like, well, "Let's go find out." We start talking to people on sites. Fortunately, the operations director is on site and we ask him, we say, tell us about opening up a new McDonald's. (00:36:54): He says, "Well, do you know we need like 120 people on opening day?" turns.speaker: Christian Idiodi
turns.en: This topic is probably near and dear to my heart because, I mean, there are many ways that I think our corporate structures have failed in creating high performance and stability in people, and I think one of them is actually encro of leadership. And by leadership, the key component I often point to is coaching. This idea of what truly is the job of a leader. And I tell people, yeah, it's context and culture at the highest level like, why are we here? Where are we going? How do we organize ourselves to get there? What's important? (00:49:51): Just kinds of things and the environment in which we do it, but there's a people element because you recognize that you want an outcome and you need people working together to that outcome. So I now have to staff those people and I have to hire and train them and equip them and then appoint them to what those things are. But many of those things are one-off, meaning I create a vision, I create a strategy. I hire a person. There's something that is every day and that's coaching, that's like the day job of managers. And if I think about high performing teams in the world, and you can pick sports is one of those, artists, they have coaches and managers like it's an everyday thing. And the idea is that when I explain this to people, I say doing product management is a product manager's job, but getting better at product management is the manager's job, is the coach's job. And people tend to misunderstand how that dynamic works. (00:50:57): You see, if you are playing a game, you're in the game. The coaches are on the sideline watching you play the game and getting you better at playing the game. Your job may be to kick or pass the ball and you need a competence level, but somebody's job is every day looking for ways for you to be better at your job. (00:51:16): The number one reason most people don't give good coaching is because they've never experienced good coaching themselves. And most people can only give to other people what has been given to them, what experiences they've seen. I was in an executive meeting with a CEO and he gets up in a meeting and he just starts screaming and cursing at everybody, just throwing up And I said, "Whoa, whoa." I said, "Can we talk outside?" They pick him outside. I was like, "First of all, I don't even think I can work with you anymore given this environment you're creating, but I need to understand why you are talking to your team like that." And he says to me, he says, "Christian, well my boss used to scream at me like this. And look at me, I'm now a CEO, I got it, I understand it. They are grownups, they can understand it too." (00:52:05): And I said, "Well, tell me what you're trying to communicate." And he explains it to me and stuff and I said, "Is it okay if I show you an alternative way of communicating that?" He says, "What do you mean?" I said, "Well is it first of all safe for me to do this with the team?" So I go back to the team and I say, "Look, I'm going to try to say what the CEO was trying to say again. He's giving me permission for you to speak freely and candidly, I want your honest opinion as to what was more effective and why." And I took a stab at kind of representing what he was trying to say and I asked the team and it's like, yeah, it's the same thing kind of message, but when he tells us this stuff we just go do it. We get it, we go do it. But the way you described it right now to us, I can think of four other things I need to do. I even understand some other things that may be missing that we need to now go tackle. (00:52:57): And the CEO is kind of really taken aback and it's kind of in some ways he has never seen an alternative. And he's never seen if an alternative be effective. Most people need to see something then they need to do it before they can even teach it, in some ways. Now I'm saying this all because I need to make a very strong argument for people understanding coaching. And in some ways I probably did not know that I was probably good at coaching. I coached my kids in soccer for eight years and we always won the championship, my boys team and I had long waiting list of people and I thought I had a fundamental flaw in understanding it because when my kids were all four years old, when you have the kids run around the soccer field just kicking the ball any way, my team always had plays, they all have strategy. (00:53:49): So winning games like 10 to zero, other kids, I thought I'm like, maybe I was born in another country. I didn't know you were just meant to let them play. And I was really coaching kids and I was treating four-year-olds like adults. We're watching video, watching tape, having real... [inaudible 00:54:05] But it was so funny when you see them execute on the field. But I've kind of always had this mentality about the truest forms like companies cannot care for people, people care for people. And the representation of what is acceptable in an environment or what we do is by the leaders. Now there's some different dynamic to why that's not happening with how we promote people and the whole poor structure around that. But fundamentally, trust is a key part of doing this. And I think when I tell these people, I say, "Look, most people don't know that you know something until they test you." (00:54:50): We do it a whole lot in our environment. I ask you a question, I see how you answer and it's like I might ask you what's one plus one? It's two and now I know that one plus one is two. I don't care when you learned it. I need you to know that it's two to do my work. So it happens in everyday environment and what people fail to do is to do the learning so they get the question wrong and they lose trust. And trust is based on competence and character, there are other values like communication and concern and care, but most corporate environments, it's a competency thing. That's why you see so many companies accept people with bad communication, bad care, because they're very good at their job. So if you can demonstrate competence, you will earn some trust, at least the trust of competence from people. (00:55:44): So I kind of explained to people a whole lot that the real core of their job at first is to learn, to seek to understand before they are understood, to know what you don't know. That humility and ego only last a small minute. The most powerful way I have found to get trust with many people is to have them accountable for an outcome of mine, which is to know. So if I wanted to accelerate trust with Lenny, I will ask Lenny to teach me. And I see this like an emotional intelligence, black belt technique here, but many environments, if you get into environment, it's very quickly for you to identify the power in that environment. Who is influential? Who has loudest voice and all? And there's something behind why they're powerful. Yes it is title, but if you think about why someone is called a CEO, it's because there's some competence that made someone give them the title, they are great at growing businesses, they have a good stride, whatever it is. (00:56:51): So what you do to build trust is you want that person to trust you. Okay. But the only way that person will know that they trust you is if they test you. And unfortunately many environments they do that publicly. I'm in a meeting, I ask Lenny a question. He bumps a presentation like, oh, product managers are useless. That person doesn't know anything. So here's what I do when I want to build trust, if Lenny's a new hire in my company, I take Lenny to the loudest, most influential person in the company. And I say, "Look, I just hired Lenny. Super rockstar, did all of this. But he knows nothing about that business, nothing about how we work and stuff. I will love for you to teach him some things." Now he may be like, "I'm super busy, I'm involved." (00:57:36): I say, "Look, Lenny should just hang with you. I've played his calendar for the whole week. He's just got to sit in meetings you are, quiet, observe, just by observing you, he will be a rockstar. No stress, nothing to give." Now it's impossible for this leader to sit with you for a whole week without saying things like, "So Lenny, where are you from? What do you do? Tell me about yourself." What have I now done? I forced a relationship between a very powerful, trustworthy, influential person and somebody else that doesn't have it. If you are walking around the company with this person, what is everybody going to say? Oh my goodness, you're friends with that person. I want to know Lenny because we can never get him to agree on it. So if I know Lenny, I'll be close with it. Lenny is more accessible, he's new, but how did Lenny break in? I'm extending somebody else's trust to you. Now by also making that person share in the accountability of training you or teaching you, in some ways, I am now making them accountable for your growth. It's impossible two months from now for that person to say, "Oh, Lenny doesn't do anything." Why? Because it makes them a bad teacher. So they're always going to be friendly, be like, "Oh yeah, Lenny, let's have a conversation. Don't do it like this in this way." They will prep you because it makes them look bad if you're not competent. Now, this technique accelerates relationships and trust. It's the help me teach me type of technique. It also allows them to observe the dynamics within the company, but it accelerates relationships because it's impossible for you to be in a meeting with a leader all the time without the person saying something like, "Oh yeah, hey folks, let me introduce you to Lenny." (00:59:20): Now that person is now the one introducing you to more connections within the company. Fastest way to build is, now feels like it's a expense but this is the job of a coach. You are designing a very specific playbook to help people achieve the outcomes reward and that's by getting them competent at their job and then their potential where they need to go next.
turns.zh: 这个话题可能是我所关心的，因为我的意思是，我认为我们的企业结构在创造高绩效和员工稳定性方面在很多方面都失败了，我认为其中之一实际上是领导力的问题。对于领导力，我经常指出的关键要素是辅导。这种关于什么是真正的领导者工作的想法。我告诉人们，是的，这是最高层次的背景和文化，比如我们为什么在这里？我们要去哪里？我们如何组织自己才能实现这一目标？什么是重要的？ (00:49:51)：只是各种事情和我们做事的环境，但其中有一个人的因素，因为你认识到你想要一个结果，并且你需要人们共同努力以实现该结果。所以我现在必须为这些人配备人员，我必须雇用和培训他们并装备他们，然后任命他们从事这些工作。但其中许多事情都是一次性的，这意味着我创造了一个愿景，我制定了一个战略。我雇用一个人。有一些事情是每天都会发生的，那就是教练，就像经理的日常工作一样。如果我想到世界上表现出色的团队，你可以选择体育运动就是其中之一，艺术家，他们有教练和经理，就像这是一件日常的事情。我的想法是，当我向人们解释这一点时，我说进行产品管理是产品经理的工作，但在产品管理方面做得更好是经理的工作，是教练的工作。人们往往会误解这种动力是如何运作的。 (00:50:57)：你看，如果你在玩游戏，你就在游戏中。教练们会在场边看着你打比赛，并帮助你打得更好。你的工作可能是踢球或传球，你需要一定的能力水平，但有人的工作是每天寻找让你更好地完成工作的方法。 (00:51:16)：大多数人不提供良好指导的首要原因是他们自己从未经历过良好的指导。大多数人只能向别人提供他们所得到的、他们所看到的经历。我正在与一位首席执行官举行高管会议，他在会议上站起来，开始对每个人尖叫和咒骂，然后呕吐，我说，“哇，哇。”我说：“我们可以出去聊聊吗？”他们在外面接他。我当时想，“首先，考虑到你正在创造的这种环境，我什至认为我不能再与你合作了，但我需要理解你为什么要这样与你的团队交谈。”他对我说，“克里斯蒂安，我的老板曾经这样对我大喊大叫。看看我，我现在是首席执行官，我明白了，我理解了。他们是成年人，他们也能理解。” (00:52:05)：我说，“好吧，告诉我你想传达什么。”他向我解释了这一点，我说：“我可以向你展示另一种沟通方式吗？”他说：“你什么意思？”我说：“首先，我和团队一起做这件事安全吗？”所以我回到团队，我说，“听着，我将尝试再次说出首席执行官想说的话。他允许我自由和坦诚地发言，我想听听你们关于什么更有效以及为什么更有效的诚实意见。”我尝试表达他想说的话，我问了团队，他们说，是的，这是同样的信息，但当他告诉我们这些东西时，我们就去做。我们明白了，我们就去做吧。但按照你现在向我们描述的方式，我可以想到我需要做的其他四件事。我什至了解我们现在需要解决的其他一些可能缺失的事情。 (00:52:57)：首席执行官确实大吃一惊，在某些方面他从未见过其他选择。他从未见过替代方案是否有效。大多数人需要看到一些东西，然后他们需要去做，然后才能以某种方式教授它。现在我之所以这么说，是因为我需要为人们理解教练提出一个非常有力的论据。在某些方面，我可能不知道自己可能擅长执教。我指导我的孩子们踢足球八年了，我们总是赢得冠军，我的男孩队和我都有很长的等待名单，我认为我在理解这一点上有一个根本性的缺陷，因为当我的孩子们四岁的时候，当你让孩子们在足球场上跑来跑去，以任何方式踢球时，我的球队总是有比赛，他们都有策略。 (00:53:49)：所以赢得像 10 比 0 这样的比赛，其他孩子，我想，也许我出生在另一个国家。我不知道你只是想让他们玩。我实际上是在指导孩子们，我像对待成年人一样对待四岁的孩子。我们正在看视频，看磁带，有真正的... [听不清 00:54:05] 但是当你看到他们在球场上执行时，这真是太有趣了。但我一直对最真实的形式抱有这样的心态，比如公司不能关心人，而是人关心人。环境中可接受的内容或我们所做的事情是由领导者代表的。现在有一些不同的动力来解释为什么我们如何晋升人员以及围绕它的整个糟糕的结构没有发生这种情况。但从根本上来说，信任是做到这一点的关键部分。我想当我告诉这些人时，我会说，“看，大多数人在测试你之前都不知道你知道一些事情。” (00:54:50)：我们在我们的环境中经常这样做。我问你一个问题，我看你如何回答，就像我可能会问你一加一是多少？是二，现在我知道一加一等于二。我不在乎你什么时候学会的。我需要你知道我的工作需要两个人来完成。因此，这种情况发生在日常环境中，而人们未能做的就是进行学习，因此他们会回答错误的问题并失去信任。信任是基于能力和品格，还有其他价值观，如沟通、关心和照顾，但在大多数企业环境中，这是一个能力问题。这就是为什么你会看到这么多公司接受沟通不善、照顾不好的人，因为他们非常擅长自己的工作。因此，如果你能够表现出能力，你就会赢得一些信任，至少是人们对能力的信任。 (00:55:44)：所以我向人们解释了很多，他们工作的真正核心首先是学习，在被理解之前寻求理解，知道你不知道的东西。这种谦卑和自我只能持续一小分钟。我发现获得许多人信任的最有效方法是让他们对我的结果负责，即了解。因此，如果我想加速与莱尼的信任，我会请莱尼来教我。我认为这就像情商、黑带技术，但是在很多环境中，如果你进入环境，你很快就能识别出该环境中的力量。谁有影响力？谁的声音最大？他们如此强大背后有一些原因。是的，这是头衔，但如果你想想为什么有人被称为首席执行官，那是因为有一些能力让某人授予他们这个头衔，他们擅长发展业务，他们有很大的进步，无论是什么。 (00:56:51)：因此，要建立信任，你要做的就是希望对方信任你。好的。但那个人知道他们信任你的唯一方法就是测试你。不幸的是，许多环境他们公开这样做。我正在开会，我问莱尼一个问题。他在演讲中提到，哦，产品经理没用。那个人什么都不知道。因此，当我想要建立信任时，我会这样做，如果莱尼是我公司的新员工，我会带莱尼去见公司中声音最大、最有影响力的人。我说，“听着，我刚刚聘请了莱尼。超级摇滚明星，做了这一切。但他对这项业务一无所知，对我们的工作方式一无所知。我很乐意让你教他一些东西。”现在他可能会说，“我超级忙，我很忙。” (00:57:36)：我说，“听着，莱尼应该和你在一起。我整整一周都在玩他的日历。他只需坐在你开的会议上，安静，观察，只要观察你，他就会成为摇滚明星。没有压力，没有什么可给予的。”现在，这位领导者不可能与你坐在一起整整一个星期而不说这样的话，“那么莱尼，你来自哪里？你做什么？告诉我你自己。”我现在做了什么？我强迫一个非常有权势、值得信赖、有影响力的人和其他没有这种关系的人建立关系。如果你和这个人在公司里走来走去，每个人都会说什么？天哪，你是那个人的朋友。我想了解莱尼，因为我们永远无法让他同意。所以如果我认识莱尼，我就会和它很亲近。莱尼更容易接近，他是新人，但莱尼是如何闯入的呢？我正在向你表达别人的信任。现在，通过让那个人分担培训你或教导你的责任，在某种程度上，我现在让他们对你的成长负责。从现在起两个月后，那个人不可能说：“哦，莱尼什么也没做。”为什么？因为这使他们成为一个糟糕的老师。所以他们总是会很友好，就像，“哦，是的，莱尼，我们来谈谈吧。不要这样做。”他们会帮助你做好准备，因为如果你没有能力，他们会显得很糟糕。现在，这项技术可以促进关系和信任。它帮助我教我一种技术。它还可以让他们观察公司内部的动态，但它可以加速人际关系，因为你不可能一直在与领导者开会，而对方不会说“哦，嘿，伙计们，让我把你介绍给莱尼。” (00:59:20)：现在这个人就是向您介绍公司内更多人脉的人。最快的构建方式是，现在感觉这是一笔开支，但这是教练的工作。您正在设计一个非常具体的剧本来帮助人们实现成果奖励，即让他们胜任自己的工作，然后发挥他们下一步需要发展的潜力。
